chicken-leg-drumstick-and-thigh-baked-co.title: Chicken leg, drumstick and thigh, baked, coated, skin/coating eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken legs, drumsticks and thighs are dark meat cuts rich in protein and healthy fats. When baked with a coating (such as breading, sauce, or marinade) they develop a flavorful crust while the skin remains edible, adding extra taste and texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dark meat contains more iron and zinc than white meat.
Baking with a coating creates a crispy crust through the Maillard reaction while keeping the meat juicy.
These cuts are staples in many cuisines, from American BBQ to Asian teriyaki dishes.
Chicken skin is a source of collagen, beneficial for skin, joints, and connective tissue.
If over‑cooked, the skin can become tough and bitter rather than crisp.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 20–25 g of complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: The meat includes monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that support heart health when eaten in moderation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Rich in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which aid energy metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for immunity, bone health, and metabolic processes.

items.title: Collagen from skin
items.content: Edible skin adds extra collagen, which may help maintain skin elasticity and joint health.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Baked, coated pieces with skin can be calorie‑rich; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Skin contains saturated fats; individuals with high cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Chicken must reach an internal temperature of at least 74 °C to eliminate salmonella and other pathogens.

items.title: Chicken protein allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium in coatings
items.content: Prepared breadings and sauces often contain added salt; choose low‑sodium options if you have hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the baked legs, drumsticks or thighs as a main dish, slice them for salads, add to soups, or use in sandwiches. The skin and coating are eaten together with the meat, providing crunch and flavor. If preferred, the skin can be removed before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw chicken refrigerated at +2–4 °C for up to 2 days. Cooked meat stores in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag at –18 °C for up to 4 months. Reheat thoroughly before consumption.

chicken-or-turkey-salad-made-with-creamy.title: Chicken or Turkey Salad with Creamy Dressing

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken or turkey salad with creamy dressing is a ready‑to‑eat mix of tender cooked poultry pieces, fresh vegetables and a flavorful creamy sauce. Perfect as a light lunch, snack or side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The creamy dressing is usually made from mayonnaise, sour cream or yogurt with added herbs and spices.
Chicken and turkey are lean sources of protein that are easy to digest.
The salad is typically kept chilled to preserve the crunch of the vegetables.
Turkey version is considered slightly more diet‑friendly due to lower fat content.
Herbs such as dill or parsley are often added to the dressing for extra aroma.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Poultry provides complete amino acids that support muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken and turkey are good sources of B6 and B12, essential for nervous system function and blood formation.

items.title: Supports immunity
items.content: The creamy dressing often contains vitamins A and D, which help strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Provides sustained energy
items.content: The combination of protein and healthy fats offers lasting satiety and steady energy levels.

items.title: Provides essential minerals
items.content: The salad supplies potassium, phosphorus and magnesium, important for heart and muscle function.

items.title: Allergy to poultry
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken or turkey, experiencing skin reactions or digestive symptoms.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Creamy dressings can be calorie‑dense and contain saturated fats; portion control is advised for weight‑watchers.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Prepared dressings often contain added salt, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: The salad must be kept refrigerated and consumed within a few days to prevent bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The salad is ready to eat straight from the package. It can be enjoyed on its own, added to a sandwich, used as a filling for wraps, or served alongside whole‑grain bread.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the product in its original packaging in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–4 days. Discard if you notice off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Raw clams are marine bivalve mollusks that live in coastal waters of seas and oceans. They have tender meat, a mildly salty flavor and a distinct sea aroma. Raw clams are often used in sushi, ceviche and as a component of cold appetizers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Clams filter water, helping to clean it of microscopic particles.
There are over 500 species of clams, but culinary use focuses mainly on members of the Veneridae family.
Clams can close their shells tightly to protect themselves from predators and adverse conditions.
In some cultures clams are considered a delicacy and are served in special ceremonies.
Clams can regenerate tissue, making them interesting subjects for biomedical research.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Clams provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many seafood items, clams contain very little fat, making them suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is crucial for nervous system function and blood formation; clams are one of the best natural sources.

items.title: Rich in minerals: iron and zinc
items.content: Clams supply iron for oxygen transport and zinc to support immune health.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Small amounts of omega‑3 in clams help promote heart health.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Raw clams may harbor pathogenic bacteria and viruses (e.g., Vibrio), so consumption requires caution.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to clams, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Heavy metal accumulation
items.content: Clams can accumulate toxins such as cadmium and mercury, especially in polluted waters.

items.title: Not recommended for pregnant women
items.content: Due to the risk of bacterial contamination, pregnant women should avoid raw clams.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw clams are typically served chilled, thinly sliced, with soy sauce, lemon, ginger or wasabi. They are also used in ceviche, where the acid “cooks” the meat. Before serving, rinse clams thoroughly in cold water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store clams in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C in a tightly sealed container covered with a damp cloth. Use within 1‑2 days. Discard any clams that remain open and do not close when gently tapped.

egg-yolk-only-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Egg, yolk only, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: The egg yolk is the yellow part of the egg that contains almost all of the nutrients, including fats, vitamins, and minerals. When cooked without added fat (e.g., boiled or steamed), it retains most of its nutritional value.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The yolk holds nearly all the fat‑soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K.
Almost all of the egg’s biologically active iron is in the yolk.
Cholesterol content is high, but current research shows moderate intake does not raise blood cholesterol for most people.
Yolk acts as a natural emulsifier in sauces, mayonnaise, and custards.
Cooking preserves most of the yolk’s antioxidant compounds.

items.title: Rich in vitamins A, D, E, and K
items.content: These vitamins support vision, immune function, bone health, and blood clotting.

items.title: High‑quality protein source
items.content: Although less than the egg white, yolk protein contains all essential amino acids.

items.title: Contains lecithin
items.content: Lecithin aids brain function and promotes liver health.

items.title: Abundant choline
items.content: Choline is vital for memory, nerve signaling, and fat metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Carotenoids such as lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from age‑related degeneration.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: People with familial hypercholesterolemia should limit yolk consumption.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to yolk proteins.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked yolk can harbor Salmonella; cook until fully set.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked yolk without added fat can be eaten on its own, added to salads, sauces, purees, or used in baking as an emulsifier.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked yolks in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in small portions.

content.title: About
content.content: A fruit smoothie is a beverage made from whole fruits without any dairy ingredients. It retains most of the fiber, vitamins, and minerals found in fresh fruit and is suitable for vegans and those with lactose intolerance.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Common blends include banana, berries, mango or pineapple, providing natural sweetness without added sugar.
Blending preserves more antioxidants compared to juicing, where much of the fiber is lost.
Fruit smoothies can be an excellent way to increase fruit intake in children who dislike eating whole fruit.
Some recipes add nut milk or oat milk for a creamier texture while staying dairy‑free.
Smoothies are often served chilled, but they can also be frozen into ice cubes for refreshing drinks.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Smoothies provide vitamin C, vitamin A, folate, and B‑vitamins that support immunity and energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Whole fruits keep the fiber intact, promoting healthy digestion and satiety.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The absence of dairy makes the drink suitable for low‑saturated‑fat diets.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Berries such as blueberries and raspberries are high in anthocyanins, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Smoothies have a high water content, contributing to overall fluid balance.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Even natural sugars can raise blood glucose levels if consumed in large portions, especially for people with diabetes.

items.title: Fruit allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to specific fruits like kiwi or strawberries.

items.title: Microbial contamination
items.content: If fruits are not washed thoroughly, bacteria or pesticide residues can end up in the smoothie.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Grapefruit can affect the metabolism of certain medications; consult a healthcare professional when using it in smoothies.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink the smoothie immediately after blending to preserve nutrients. It can replace a breakfast, serve as a snack, or act as a dessert alternative. For extra protein and healthy fats, add protein powder, chia seeds, or nut milk.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store smoothies in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Longer storage may lead to flavor loss and vitamin degradation. Shake or stir before drinking, as ingredients tend to settle.

content.title: About
content.content: Gluten‑free pancakes are light, fluffy discs made from a blend of gluten‑free flours (such as rice, buckwheat or oat), eggs, milk and a touch of oil. They are suitable for people with celiac disease or anyone following a gluten‑free diet while preserving the classic taste and texture of traditional pancakes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gluten‑free pancakes can be made with a variety of flours, each giving a distinct flavor and color.
The first documented gluten‑free pancake recipe appeared in the 1970s in the United States as gluten‑free diets gained popularity.
They are often served with berry sauces, honey, nut butter, or fresh fruit.
When the liquid‑to‑flour ratio is slightly higher than in regular pancakes, the result is a tender, airy crumb.
Gluten‑free pancakes freeze well; after thawing they can be quickly reheated on a skillet.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Gluten‑free flours contain no gluten, which can irritate the gut of people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and milk provide B12, riboflavin and niacin, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: Eggs and milk add complete protein that helps tissue repair and satiety.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: Using whole‑grain gluten‑free flours like buckwheat helps maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: A small amount of vegetable oil supplies omega‑6 fatty acids important for skin and hair health.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: The pancakes contain eggs and milk, which can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some recipes add sugar; people monitoring sugar intake should adjust the amount.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Even gluten‑free pancakes are calorie‑dense due to oil and dairy; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Cross‑contamination
items.content: Use clean utensils and surfaces to avoid accidental gluten exposure during preparation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve warm with honey, maple syrup, berry compote, low‑fat yogurt, or cottage cheese. They can be rolled with savory fillings like vegetables, ham or cheese, or used as a base for gluten‑free casseroles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked pancakes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze them on parchment‑lined trays; reheat on a skillet or in the microwave before serving.
